controls.value: Object-level authorization is enforced on every resource route
Rate limits and quotas are applied per principal
Webhooks and inter-service requests are signed and replay-protected
An API inventory exists and unknown routes are alerted on
File uploads are validated by type, size and content and stored outside the web root
Error handling never returns stack traces or internal identifiers to clients
Trust boundaries are drawn and every crossing authenticates and authorizes (truent threat-model)
Blast radius is bounded: one compromised component cannot reach the data store directly
Defaults fail closed; a missing config denies rather than allows
Internet-facing assets, subdomains and certificates are enumerated continuously and diffed
Shadow infrastructure is reconciled against the asset inventory
Backups are automated, immutable, versioned and geographically separated
Restores are tested on a schedule and the last test date is recorded
Database snapshots are taken before every migration
CSPM continuously evaluates the live account against a benchmark (CIS); IaC findings here are the pre-deploy half
Cloud IAM permissions are reviewed for excess and unused grants (CIEM)
Cloud audit logging is enabled in every account and region and shipped off-account
Images are scanned for CVEs and signed before admission (cosign/sigstore)
Runtime profiles (seccomp, AppArmor) and read-only root filesystems are enforced
Data is classified and the classification drives encryption, retention and access
Field-level encryption or tokenization covers regulated fields
DLP controls cover endpoints, email and cloud storage for classified data
Database roles follow least privilege; the application role cannot alter schema
Row-level security or tenant scoping is enforced in the database, not only the application
Database activity is audited and backups are encrypted
Detections exist for suspicious login, privilege escalation, credential abuse, exfiltration, persistence and lateral movement, each mapped to ATT&CK
Every detection has a tested, documented response
truent scan --chain auto, truent deps and truent gate run on every pull request and block on Critical/High
Branch protection requires review and passing checks; force-push to protected branches is disabled
MFA or passkeys are required for every human account; privileged access is just-in-time
Service accounts and workload identities use short-lived credentials, not static keys
RBAC/ABAC policies are reviewed quarterly for excess privilege
Isolation, credential revocation and attacker blocking each have a rehearsed runbook and an owner
Evidence is preserved before remediation (logs, images, traces)
truent-ir covers on-chain incidents; SOAR playbooks cover accounts, endpoints and containers
Pod Security Standards (restricted) are enforced by an admission controller
Kubernetes RBAC grants no cluster-admin to workloads; service-account tokens are not auto-mounted
Secrets are stored in an external manager, not in plain Secret objects
Egress is restricted by allowlist; workloads cannot reach arbitrary internet hosts
Service-to-service traffic is mutually authenticated (mTLS / service mesh)
IDS/IPS or flow monitoring covers every network segment
Web, API, cloud and internal tests are performed at least annually and after major changes; findings feed the regression corpus
Rate limiting, circuit breakers and backpressure protect every public entry point
Failover is automated and RTO/RPO are measured, not assumed
EDR covers servers and developer machines; container runtime security (Falco/Tetragon) alerts on shells, unexpected processes and outbound connections
WAF/RASP fronts web applications with rules tuned to the application
Artifacts are signed and carry build provenance (SLSA); an SBOM ships with every release (truent deps --sbom)
Commits are signed and builds are reproducible
Findings are prioritized by exploitability (EPSS/KEV) and tracked to closure with SLAs by severity
Patches are verified by re-scan, not by ticket state
HSTS, CSP and the standard security headers are set and verified in production responses
A WAF and bot/DDoS protection front the site

attack_chains.name: Session hijack over cleartext
attack_chains.narrative: An attacker on the path (public Wi-Fi, a compromised router) waits for the victim to load the site over plain HTTP, which is served without redirecting; the session cookie, lacking Secure, is sent in the clear and replayed.

attack_chains.name: Credentials served to the internet
attack_chains.narrative: A configuration or repository file is fetched anonymously from the web root; it contains credentials that the attacker uses directly against the database, cloud account or third-party API.

attack_chains.name: Injection reaching a reachable database
attack_chains.narrative: Untrusted input reaches a query; the database it runs against is publicly addressable or unencrypted, so the injection turns into bulk read of the store rather than a single-row leak.

attack_chains.name: CI takeover becomes a supply-chain compromise
attack_chains.narrative: A pull request from a fork runs with repository secrets (pwn request / script injection); the attacker exfiltrates the publishing token, or edits an unpinned action, and ships a poisoned release to every downstream user.

steps.role: secrets or publish path in reach

attack_chains.name: Stored/reflected XSS to account takeover
attack_chains.narrative: Script injected through an HTML sink runs in the victim's browser unrestricted by a CSP; the session cookie is readable by script (no HttpOnly) and is sent to the attacker.

attack_chains.name: SSRF to cloud metadata credentials
attack_chains.narrative: A server-side fetch of an attacker-chosen URL is pointed at the cloud metadata service; the returned role credentials are used with a wildcard IAM policy to take over the account.

attack_chains.name: Command injection to host compromise
attack_chains.narrative: A command injection gives code execution inside the container; the container runs as root and privileged (or with host namespaces), so the process escapes to the node.

attack_chains.name: Unauthenticated service reachable from the internet
attack_chains.narrative: A database or cache port is open to the world (observed live) and the infrastructure code that allowed it is in the repository; default-unauthenticated services are read and written directly.

attack_chains.name: Adversary-in-the-middle on a client that skips TLS verification
attack_chains.narrative: A client disables certificate verification; an on-path attacker presents any certificate, terminates TLS, and reads the credentials or tokens the client sends.

attack_chains.name: Flash-loan oracle manipulation to protocol drain
attack_chains.narrative: A flash loan moves the spot price the contract reads in the same transaction; with no post-state solvency check, the attacker borrows or mints against the inflated value and repays the loan with the protocol's funds.

attack_chains.name: Reentrancy with unchecked external calls
attack_chains.narrative: An external call is made before state is updated and its return value is not checked; a malicious receiver re-enters and withdraws repeatedly.

attack_chains.name: Single admin key to full protocol control
attack_chains.narrative: One externally-owned key controls upgrades or privileged functions with no timelock; the key is phished or leaked (it may already be in the repository) and the attacker upgrades to a draining implementation instantly.
